passage:
Dear Sharmila,

I owe you and the team an apology. For two weeks I told myself I was saving time by doing the project alone. I stayed up until two most nights cutting, gluing and writing the report, because I thought nobody else would do it right. By Thursday my eyes were burning and I got the scale wrong on the base. Nobody noticed, because nobody had been asked. You offered to help twice and I said, "It's fine." I know that must have made you feel unneeded. The model looks rough now, and none of you knows it well enough to explain it. I made it worse by refusing help. Can we sit down on Monday and split up what's left?

Akash

qa.q: Until what time did Akash stay up on most nights?
qa.a: Akash stayed up until two on most nights.

qa.q: How does Akash feel now about refusing help?
qa.a: Akash feels regretful and worn out, admitting the refusal made things worse and left the team unable to explain the model.

qa.q: What could Akash have done instead of working alone, and why?
qa.a: Akash could have split the tasks at the start and checked in on progress, because shared work keeps quality up and lets everyone learn.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when the offers of help were turned down?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt sidelined and unneeded, since two offers of help were refused with 'It's fine.'

grounding: Not trusting others, the leader does most of the work at night and gets exhausted, the team feels sidelined, the quality drops and members learn nothing from the project.

subtype: Approach: leaving it to the last week [Pitfall]
passage: Yusuf's group had three weeks to build a model water purifier and assumed there was plenty of time. They met once, in the first week, to choose a design, and never fixed dates. In week three, Ishita's family left for a wedding in another city and another member came down with a fever, so by Wednesday only Yusuf and one other were left. The exhibition was on Friday. On Thursday night Yusuf glued the tubes while Ishita, back late, painted the base. The label was crooked and one tube leaked. On Friday a judge asked how the filter worked, and Yusuf gave a half answer while water dripped onto the table. Ishita looked at her shoes.

qa.q: How often did the group meet in the first three weeks?
qa.a: The group met only once, in the first week.

qa.q: What might Yusuf be feeling as water dripped while the judge waited?
qa.a: Yusuf is probably embarrassed and frustrated, giving a half answer while the leak shows the rush.

qa.q: What could the group have done at the start, and why?
qa.a: They could have set dates for each stage and short check-ins, because a plan with dates shows problems early, before absences hit.

qa.q: How might Ishita see the finished model?
qa.a: Ishita likely feels guilty and awkward, having missed part of the work, which is why Ishita looked at the shoes.

grounding: The group assumes there is plenty of time and meets only once, and in the final week two members are absent and the model is finished in a rush with obvious flaws.

subtype: Approach: setting shared rules and check-ins [Action]
passage:
Madhav: Before we start: rules. Two check-ins a week, ten minutes, Tuesday and Friday at lunch.
Varun: Ten minutes? That's nothing.
Madhav: That's the point. Everyone says what's done, what's next, what's stuck.
Varun: And a chat group?
Madhav: I already made "Bridge Team." One more rule: if you're stuck, say so by the next check-in. Not the day before the deadline.
Varun: What if I'm embarrassed to say I'm stuck?
Madhav: Then say "I need ten minutes of help." That's all. Nobody counts.
Varun: Fine. Actually I'm already stuck on the load table. I can't find the formula.
Madhav: See? Tuesday I'll bring my notes. Two minutes, done.
Varun: Okay. This might actually work.

qa.q: On which days are the check-ins?
qa.a: The check-ins are on Tuesday and Friday at lunch.

qa.q: How does Varun feel about admitting being stuck?
qa.a: Varun feels embarrassed at the thought, though Varun does admit being stuck on the load table.

qa.q: What could the team do if someone misses a check-in, and why?
qa.a: They could message the person in the chat that day, because an early nudge finds a problem before it becomes a deadline crisis.

qa.q: How does Madhav see a member who is stuck?
qa.a: Madhav sees it as normal and easy to fix, saying nobody counts the times, so asking for ten minutes of help is fine.

grounding: The team agrees on twice-weekly ten-minute check-ins, a common chat group and a rule that anyone stuck says so early, so problems surface before they become deadline crises.

subtype: Approach: handling a member who is not contributing [Action]
passage: Tejas had not handed in anything for two weeks. At the team meeting the others exchanged looks and the room felt tight. I could have said, "Tejas, where's your part?" in front of everyone. Instead I waited until after class and walked with him to the gate. "I'm not checking up on you," I said. "I just wondered if something's in the way." Tejas looked at his shoes and said the model needed card, glue and paint, and there was none at home. I hadn't guessed that at all. I asked whether he would take the research and the report, which needed only a library book and a notebook, and let Anita handle the materials. His shoulders came down. Two days later he brought four pages of notes. I'm Chandrika, and I'm glad I asked quietly.

qa.q: What did Tejas say was in the way?
qa.a: Tejas said the model needed card, glue and paint, and there was none at home.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when Chandrika asked quietly at the gate?
qa.a: Tejas felt embarrassed at first, looking at his shoes, then relieved, as his shoulders came down.

qa.q: What else could Chandrika do to help Tejas feel part of the team, and why?
qa.a: Chandrika could ask Tejas to present the research at the next check-in, because owning a real part lets Tejas show what Tejas contributes.

qa.q: How might the other team members have seen Tejas's silence before the talk?
qa.a: They probably thought Tejas did not care and felt annoyed, since nobody knew the real reason.

grounding: The leader speaks privately to the quiet member, asks what is blocking him, finds he lacks materials, and shifts him to research he can do at home, without shaming him in front of others.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version and iteration [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Thomas looked at the plan for a model water lift: pulleys, buckets, a motor, a painted base. Too much for two weeks. He wrote: "Version one: one pulley, one bucket, a hand crank. It only has to lift water." Deepak wanted the motor first. "If we finish nothing, the motor doesn't matter," Thomas said.

Wednesday: The crank version lifted a cup of water, slowly and with a wobble. They showed it to the teacher, who said the string kept slipping and the bucket was too heavy.

Saturday: With that feedback they fixed the string, swapped the bucket, and only then added the second pulley. The motor stayed a plan for next time.

qa.q: What did the first version of the water lift have?
qa.a: It had one pulley, one bucket and a hand crank.

qa.q: What does Thomas think about aiming for a perfect model, and how does he feel about it?
qa.a: Thomas thinks a perfect model might never be finished, and feels sensible and determined to get something working first.

qa.q: What could the group do if the teacher's feedback asks for a big change, and why?
qa.a: They could pick the one fix that matters most and do that first, because small steady improvements keep a working version alive.

qa.q: How might Deepak see leaving the motor for later?
qa.a: Deepak may feel disappointed at first, having wanted the motor, but seeing a working crank version likely makes waiting easier.

grounding: The group first builds a simple working version, shows it to the teacher for feedback, and then improves features, instead of aiming for a perfect model that may not be finished in time.

subtype: Approach: groupthink on a weak idea [Pitfall]
passage: In the school workshop in Da Nang, Tuan laid a sketch on the table: a bridge of wooden sticks with one tall arch and no side supports. "This will hold the most weight," he said, and everyone nodded. Nadia frowned at the arch, which looked thin at the base, but said nothing. Linh glanced at Nadia and bit her lip. On test day the arch bowed and cracked under the second weight. The team stared at the pile of sticks. "I thought it might," Nadia said at last. "So did I," said Linh. Tuan looked from one to the other. "Then why did nobody say so?" No one answered. Each of them had thought someone else would speak first.

qa.q: Where was the bridge test held and what happened to the arch?
qa.a: The arch bowed and cracked under the second weight on test day.

qa.q: Why did Nadia stay silent when the plan was shown?
qa.a: Nadia felt doubtful but hesitant to object, probably not wanting to be the only one to disagree with a confident plan.

qa.q: What could the team do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: They could ask each member for a concern before choosing a design, because that lets doubts be voiced without anyone standing alone.

qa.q: How might Tuan feel when learning that two people had doubts?
qa.a: Tuan probably feels surprised and a little hurt, since a concern could have saved the bridge.

grounding: Everyone agrees with the confident member's plan even though two have doubts, the design fails at testing, and the team later admits nobody wanted to be the one to object.

subtype: Approach: inviting dissent and choosing by criteria [Revision]
passage: After our model failed, I changed how we chose the next design. I asked Preeti and each of the other three to say one concern about every idea, out loud, before any vote. At first it felt awkward. Preeti said the second idea needed glue that took two days to dry. Someone else said the tower might not fit through the classroom door. Then we scored each idea from one to five on cost, time and whether it could really be built. The confident idea, the one I had loved, got a low score on feasibility, which surprised me. The plainest idea won. It was not exciting, but it stood up at the test. I'm Sharmila, and I've learned to ask before I decide.

qa.q: How did the group score each idea?
qa.a: They scored each idea from one to five on cost, time and whether it could really be built.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when the loved idea scored low?
qa.a: Sharmila was surprised and a little disappointed, since Sharmila had loved that idea.

qa.q: What could Sharmila add for the next decision, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could ask a teacher to review the shortlist before the final vote, because an outside view catches problems the group cannot see.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about being asked for a concern?
qa.a: Preeti probably felt relieved to be invited to speak, since the concern about glue drying time was heard and used.

grounding: After the failure, the leader asks each member to state one concern and scores ideas on cost, time and feasibility, so the next decision uses evidence rather than confidence.

subtype: Approach: reflecting and reallocating after a missed milestone [Revision]
passage: Thursday night. First deadline missed today: the circuit board isn't wired. Feeling flat. Instead of blaming anyone, at lunch I sat with Divyansh and the others and asked why. Honest answers: I gave the wiring one afternoon and it needs three. The report looked small but takes an evening. We all guessed low for the hard parts and high for the easy ones. New plan: wiring gets three afternoons, Divyansh moves from decoration to help with wiring, the report gets two evenings shared between us. The teacher agreed to move the deadline by four days. Still tired, but not panicky. Small win: nobody was blamed, and everybody knows their share. - Sabina

qa.q: How many afternoons does the wiring now get?
qa.a: The wiring now gets three afternoons.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel at the end of the diary entry?
qa.a: Sabina feels tired but calmer and not panicky, and pleased that nobody was blamed.

qa.q: What could the team do to avoid missing the next deadline, and why?
qa.a: They could estimate the hard parts first and add extra time for them, because the missed deadline came from guessing low on the difficult tasks.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel about moving from decoration to wiring?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel a mix of challenge and importance, since the harder job matters more to the deadline.

grounding: When the first deadline is missed, the team looks at why, finds tasks were underestimated, and redistributes work with more time allowed for the harder parts.

subtype: Approach: documenting and understanding what is happening [Thinking]
passage: Note, school counsellor, Tuesday. Salma came to my room at lunch with a notebook and asked if I had five minutes. She had written down dates, times and the wording of each message from the class group chat, and taped screenshots onto three pages. "I didn't know how to say it," she said. "This is easier." For three weeks she had been teased online about the way she talks. I listened, told her it was not her fault, and thanked her for bringing it. What I did: photographed the record with her permission, told the safeguarding lead that same afternoon, and phoned her parents with Salma in the room. I also informed her class teacher, Seema, and we agreed to speak to Salma again on Thursday.

qa.q: How many pages of screenshots did Salma tape into the notebook?
qa.a: Salma taped screenshots onto three pages.

qa.q: What might Salma have felt about bringing the notebook, and how do we know?
qa.a: Salma was probably anxious and relieved to have a way to explain, shown by saying 'I didn't know how to say it' and 'This is easier.'

qa.q: What did the counsellor do to make sure the problem was handled safely?
qa.a: The counsellor told Salma it was not her fault, photographed the record with permission, and informed the safeguarding lead, the parents and the class teacher the same day.

qa.q: How might Salma's parents have felt when phoned?
qa.a: Her parents were probably worried and upset for Salma but glad to be told, so they can support Salma at home. 🤍

grounding: A student being teased online notes dates, messages and screenshots, recognising that a clear record turns a hard-to-describe feeling into something adults can act on.

passage: On Sunday evening in the kasba, Jeevan spread his notebook on the kitchen table in front of Papa. Harish read the dates, the times and the messages from the class group, the names, the laughing at Jeevan's torn bag. He read slowly. "You did well to keep this," Harish said. "None of it is your fault." Jeevan's shoulders eased. On Monday morning Papa walked into school with him. The class teacher went through the pages, thanked him, and took them to the counsellor before lunch. By afternoon the headmaster had called a meeting under the school's anti-bullying policy, the parents of the boys involved were sent for, and a teacher would sit in the class for the next weeks. Jeevan was no longer alone with it.

qa.q: Whom did Jeevan show the notebook to on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Jeevan showed the notebook to Papa, Harish, at the kitchen table.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after Papa said none of it was his fault?
qa.a: Jeevan felt relieved, as his shoulders eased, no longer carrying the blame or the secret.

qa.q: What else could Jeevan do if the messages continued after the meeting, and why?
qa.a: Jeevan could tell the class teacher or counsellor again the same day and keep adding to the record, because the policy gives the school a way to act again.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see the notebook?
qa.a: The class teacher sees clear, dated evidence that can be acted on, and is grateful Jeevan brought it, which is why it went to the counsellor before lunch.

grounding: The student shows the record to a parent and the class teacher, who involve the school counsellor and follow the anti-bullying policy, so the target does not carry the problem alone.
